lesson.title: Conjugation Roots & The Living Endings
lesson.subtitle: Why Shakespeare's 'thou -st' and archaic '-th' unlock German verb conjugations

hook.title: Shakespeare's Hidden Conjugation Table
hook.content: English speakers often view verb conjugation tables as an unnatural obstacle. But German verb endings are not foreign: they are the exact personal suffixes English used until the 17th century! Early Modern English preserved 'thou -st' (thou learnst, thou drinkst) and 3rd person '-th' (he learneth, he cometh). German simply kept these living endings intact.

footnotes.title: Proto-Germanic Personal Inflections
footnotes.content: Ancient Germanic marked the grammatical subject directly on the verb root via distinct personal suffixes.

pattern.title: Stem + Suffix: The Universal Formula
pattern.content: Strip the dictionary infinitive '-en' to find the bare verb stem (lern-, trink-, mach-). Then attach the personal tile: 'ich -e' (Old English ic binde), 'du -st' (Early Modern English thou learnst / thou drinkst), 'er/sie/es -t' (archaic he learneth / he drinketh), 'wir -en' (Middle English we drinken), 'ihr -t' (plural y'all), and 'sie -en' (they). Once you recognize Shakespeare in 'du trinkst' and 'er trinkt', you never have to memorize a regular verb table again!

footnotes.title: Thou -st ↔ Du -st
footnotes.content: 2nd person singular '-st' is an identical historical cognate across both languages.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the verb form for 'thou makest / you make' (Stem + Shakespearean ending):
exercises.explanation: Stem 'mach-' + 2nd person singular suffix '-st' (twin of Early Modern English 'thou -st') = machst.

exercises.prompt: Match each thought with its German form — the ending carries the person:
exercises.target_answer: du stehst, er zeigt, du küsst, wir küssen, wir stehen, du machst
exercises.meaning: you stand, he shows, you kiss, we kiss, we stand, you make
exercises.explanation: The person lives in the ending: du takes the Shakespearean -st, er the archaic -t, wir the full dictionary -en — stehen, zeigen and küssen just wear them.

exercises.prompt: In 'Wir spazieren und wir fotografieren', why do both verbs end in -en?
options: Because wir takes the dictionary -en — the full ending returns for we
Because they are Latin loans and keep their own rules
exercises.target_answer: Because wir takes the dictionary -en — the full ending returns for we
exercises.meaning: the wir-form is the dictionary form at work
exercises.explanation: Strip nothing: with wir the verb IS its dictionary self — spazieren, fotografieren, lernen, kommen. The ending you add for ich is the only one that ever shrinks.

exercises.prompt: The shop mirror: 'Wir wollen es _____' (to try on — complete the bracket infinitive):
exercises.english_hint: an + probieren — inside the bracket the separable verb stays whole
exercises.meaning: Wir wollen es anprobieren = we want to try it on
exercises.explanation: The modal bracket from topic 2 keeps the separable verb whole: anprobieren closes it, prefix and all — and anprobieren is 'probe' wearing its Latin papers.

exercises.idea: you're describing your household's morning split: you make the coffee and we drink the tea
cues: Endings do the work: du machst (thou makest), wir trinken (we drinken)
und joins two full clauses — each verb holds its own position 2
exercises.target_answer: Du machst Kaffee und wir trinken Tee
exercises.meaning: You make coffee and we drink tea
exercises.explanation: Subject + conjugated verb, twice over: the endings carry the persons across both clauses.

diagnosis.cue: du keeps the Shakespearean -st: du machst (thou makest), du trinkst (thou drinkest). English only dropped it in the 1600s — German never did.

summary.outcome: Conjugate a regular present-tense verb for ich, du, er/sie/es, and wir.

use_example.german: Du machst Kaffee und wir trinken Tee.
use_example.english: You make coffee and we drink tea.

summary.takeaway: German present tense endings directly preserve the ancestral English system: ich -e, du -st, er -t, wir -en.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the stem hunters — strip -en at speed and rebuild every person of a verb from its stem.

twist.prompt: The camera changes hands: ich fotografiere → we photograph. Put it in German.
twist.explanation: ich -e → wir -en: the -ieren stamp never moves, only the personal ending does — fotografieren is a Latin loan taking German endings like any native verb.

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

denken.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Shares the exact vowel-shift relationship with "danken" that English has in "think" and "thank" (a thank is a good thought).

finden.context_translation: I cannot find it / I find it not.
finden.etymology_derivation: Stem find + infinitive -en (German keeps pure short [ɪ] vowel).

singen.etymology_derivation: Initial S voiced to [z] before vowels.

bringen.etymology_derivation: Shared ancient Germanic mixed verb (bring/brought ↔ bringen/gebracht).

du.etymology_derivation: Direct cognate of archaic English "thou". Conjugates with -st (thou goest ↔ du gehst).

stehen.context_phrase: Ich stehe am Fenster und sehe hinaus.
stehen.context_translation: I stand at the window and look out.
stehen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *stāną; the page documents cognate English stand, the same stand-verb family (English stood, German stand). [wiktionary]

zeigen.context_phrase: Kannst du mir den Weg zeigen?
zeigen.context_translation: Can you show me the way?
zeigen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German zeigōn, an intensive of zīhan; the page traces it to PIE *deyḱ- and notes that the root also gave Zeichen and English teach. The t of teach corresponds to the z of zeigen. [wiktionary]

küssen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *kussijan — English kiss is the documented cognate; a doubled expressive kk that both languages kept. [wiktionary]

fotografieren.context_translation: We are photographing the old houses.
fotografieren.etymology_derivation: A Greek-rooted international word in the -ieren loan-verb family; like all -ieren verbs its participle takes no ge-: fotografiert. [wiktionary]

anprobieren.context_translation: I would like to try on the jacket.
anprobieren.etymology_derivation: an- + probieren (to try), from Latin probare - a verb of the French-derived -ieren family; as a separable verb it keeps ge- inside: anprobiert. [wiktionary]

spazieren.english_cognate: to stroll, go for a walk
spazieren.english_meaning: to stroll, go for a walk
spazieren.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian spaziare, from Latin spatiari, to stroll — an -ieren verb; English space is from the same Latin spatium. [wiktionary]

sportplatz.context_phrase: Die Kinder spielen auf dem Sportplatz.
sportplatz.context_translation: The children play on the sports field.
sportplatz.etymology_derivation: Sport + Platz — the sports field; both elements are shared loans (Sport, Platz/place). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
